name: Pricing Illiquid Assets
title: Pricing Illiquid Assets
answer: Pricing illiquid assets covers the estimation of fair value for positions that do not trade on an active market, such as private equity, private credit, real estate, infrastructure, venture capital, and thinly traded securities. In portfolio construction, these prices feed risk models, performance attribution, capital allocation, and reporting to investors. The work sits between accounting fair value rules, market practice, and quantitative modeling, because no single observable price settles the question. The scope includes both periodic valuation for financial statements and more frequent estimates for internal risk and allocation decisions.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: What it runs on is a data infrastructure that combines internal deal records, capital account statements, fund administrator reports, and cash flow histories with external market data. Public comparables, credit spreads, yield curves, real estate indices, and transaction databases supply the observable anchors. The site's 117 listed AI-related instruments with daily prices can serve as one source of public comparables for AI-linked private positions, while the 354 merger and acquisition filings can inform precedent transaction analysis. Compute runs on cloud or on-premise clusters for Monte Carlo simulation, scenario analysis, and model training, with version control and data lineage tools to track inputs. Spreadsheets remain common for smaller portfolios, but larger shops use valuation platforms and data warehouses.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: How the work is done: analysts and portfolio managers start with the contractual cash flows and the seniority of the claim, then choose a valuation approach such as discounted cash flow, market multiples, or option pricing models. They calibrate discount rates from observable market data, adjust for illiquidity, control, and concentration, and run sensitivity tests around key assumptions. Machine learning can help select comparable companies, estimate private market betas, or detect stale pricing, but it usually supports rather than replaces the valuation committee's judgment. The output is a range of values, not a single point, and the range is documented with the assumptions that drive it. Regular backtesting against subsequent financing rounds, exits, or write-downs helps test whether the process is well calibrated.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance: valuation inputs often carry confidentiality obligations, so access controls, data licensing terms, and restrictions on material non-public information matter. Firms need a documented valuation policy, an independent review or valuation committee, and an audit trail that shows who changed which assumption and when. Provenance covers the source of every input, from a broker quote to a fund administrator's net asset value to a model-generated comparable set. The site's 219 compliance and regulation pages and 148 active AI lawsuits illustrate the broader regulatory and litigation context that can affect how AI-related private assets are valued and disclosed. Model risk management, conflict of interest checks, and clear escalation paths are part of the control environment.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Where it is going: more frequent and more data-driven valuation, as private markets grow and investors ask for daily or monthly estimates rather than quarterly marks. AI tools are likely to improve comparable selection, document parsing, and scenario generation, while regulators push for greater transparency and consistency. Secondary markets, continuation vehicles, and tokenized funds may create new price signals for assets that were once entirely appraisal-based. The main tension will remain between timely estimates and reliable evidence, because a model can produce a number quickly but cannot manufacture a market. Expect continued blending of human judgment, market data, and machine learning, with governance keeping pace.
